## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, the enriched biological pathways associated with depression are ranked according to statistical significance and biological relevance. A prominent pattern is the recurrence of immune-related and inflammatory signaling terms. Among the strongest signals are receptor complex (Gene Ontology: GO:0043235, P < 2.05 × 10−9), Signaling by Interleukins (Reactome: R-HSA-449147, P < 1.68 × 10−3), Other interleukin signaling (Reactome: R-HSA-449836, P < 1.41 × 10−2), Cytokines and inflammatory response (WikiPathways: WP530, P < 1.81 × 10−4), and Rheumatoid arthritis (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 05323, P < 3.38 × 10−6). Taken together, these results suggest that inflammatory receptor biology and interleukin-mediated signaling may represent a central organizing theme in the enrichment profile. This interpretation is consistent with a substantial body of literature indicating that depression is often accompanied by increased inflammatory cytokine activity, altered interleukin signaling, and abnormal immune receptor function, all of which may influence neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, and stress responsiveness. In the same general direction, the enrichment of the interferon regulatory factor motif (Transcription Factor: M08887_1, P < 4.06 × 10−2) may further support the possible involvement of innate immune transcriptional programs that have repeatedly been associated with depressive symptoms.

Building on this immune-centered pattern, the enrichment results also point toward transcriptional stress-response and cellular damage pathways. In particular, the p53 motif (Transcription Factor: M10023_1, P < 1.10 × 10−2) is enriched, which may suggest a contribution from apoptotic regulation, cellular senescence, and stress-induced transcriptional activity to depression pathophysiology. This interpretation appears biologically plausible because chronic stress and inflammation can activate p53-related programs, which may in turn impair neuronal survival and synaptic resilience. Alongside this observation, the enrichment of regulation of lipid metabolic process (Gene Ontology: GO:0019216, P < 1.66 × 10−2) is also noteworthy, as it is compatible with growing evidence that disturbed lipid metabolism may influence membrane composition, inflammatory tone, and brain signaling in depression.

A further layer of interpretation emerges from pathways related to mucosal and peripheral immune homeostasis. Intestinal immune network for immunoglobulin A production (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 04672, P < 1.02 × 10−4), colon goblet cell signatures from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA:0130893, P < 4.82 × 10−8; HPA:0130892, P < 4.69 × 10−8), epithelial structure maintenance (Gene Ontology: GO:0010669, P < 2.70 × 10−3), cargo receptor activity (Gene Ontology: GO:0038024, P < 2.77 × 10−5), and late endosome (Gene Ontology: GO:0005770, P < 1.63 × 10−2) collectively suggest possible involvement of barrier integrity, vesicular trafficking, and gut-associated immune regulation. In this context, these findings may be compatible with literature implicating the gut-brain axis, epithelial dysfunction, and altered immune trafficking in subsets of patients with depression.

Although several additional phenotype and disease annotations appear less specific to depression itself, they may still reflect overlapping biological processes that are relevant to the broader enrichment pattern. For example, bone pain (Human Phenotype Ontology: HP:0002653, P < 6.54 × 10−3), splenomegaly (Human Phenotype Ontology: HP:0001744, P < 6.54 × 10−3), pleural mesothelioma (WikiPathways: WP5087, P < 4.71 × 10−3), and virus receptor activity (Gene Ontology: GO:0001618, P < 2.61 × 10−2) may indicate shared inflammatory, proliferative, or host-defense mechanisms rather than direct disease-specific effects. Overall, the strongest signals in Table 1 support a model in which depression may be linked to convergent abnormalities in immune-interleukin signaling, inflammatory receptor biology, stress-responsive transcriptional control, lipid regulation, and mucosal immune homeostasis. The very small P values observed for several pathways, including 2.043 × 10−9 for receptor complex and 4.687 × 10−8 to 4.819 × 10−8 for colon goblet cell signatures, provide statistical support for the potential interconnection of these mechanisms.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Factor: IRF; motif: NNGAAANTGAAANN; match class: 1 (TF:M08887_1) 

Interferon regulatory factor pathway activity refers to transcriptional control mediated by members of the interferon regulatory factor family binding to a conserved deoxyribonucleic acid sequence characterized here by the motif NNGAAANTGAAANN. Interferon regulatory factors are sequence-specific transcription factors that are central regulators of innate immune signaling, antiviral defense, inflammatory cytokine production, antigen presentation, and crosstalk between immune and stress-responsive gene programs. These factors are activated downstream of pattern-recognition receptors, cytokine receptors, and intracellular nucleic acid sensing systems, and they control the expression of interferons, interferon-stimulated genes, and multiple inflammatory mediators. Because the motif contains repeated guanine-adenine-adenine elements typical of interferon regulatory factor recognition, this pathway is best understood as a transcriptional regulatory module that integrates immune challenge with durable changes in gene expression. In the nervous system and peripheral immune compartment, interferon regulatory factor signaling can influence microglial activation, leukocyte inflammatory tone, cytokine release, blood-brain barrier communication, synaptic remodeling, neuroendocrine regulation, and neuronal plasticity. Collectively, these processes are biologically relevant to depression, particularly in forms of illness associated with chronic inflammation, stress-induced immune activation, and altered neuroimmune communication.

Against this biological background, the disease relevance of the pathway can be considered, while still remaining appropriately cautious given the evidence provided. No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a publication-supported pathway-to-disease analysis cannot be established from the supplied evidence set. Nevertheless, from a biological standpoint, the interferon regulatory factor transcriptional program is plausibly related to depression because depression is frequently associated with activation of innate immune pathways, increased inflammatory cytokine signaling, and downstream changes in brain function that affect mood, motivation, sleep, and cognition. Interferon regulatory factor proteins occupy an upstream position in these immune cascades by regulating interferon production and broader inflammatory gene expression; therefore, persistent or dysregulated activation of this pathway could contribute to a pro-inflammatory state that promotes microglial reactivity, perturbs synaptic homeostasis, alters monoaminergic and glutamatergic signaling, and disrupts neuroplastic processes implicated in depression. In addition, inflammatory signaling controlled by interferon regulatory factors may interact with hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction and stress biology, thereby linking peripheral immune activation to central depressive symptoms. However, because no publications were supplied, these statements should be regarded as mechanism-based interpretation rather than a direct literature-derived conclusion for this specific pathway.

To complement this mechanistic interpretation, the enrichment result provides a quantitative indication of pathway involvement within the depression-associated protein set. There were 127 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of interferon regulatory factor pathway activity, a transcriptional regulatory program defined by binding to the conserved deoxyribonucleic acid motif NNGAAANTGAAANN. This protein set of 127 supports a quantitatively substantial enrichment signal and is biologically consistent with the central role of interferon regulatory factor-mediated transcription in innate immune signaling, antiviral defense, inflammatory cytokine production, antigen presentation, and immune-to-neural communication, all of which are highly relevant to depression, particularly in inflammatory and stress-associated disease states. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 127 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network exploration.

With this network context in place, the following section introduces several of the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and considers their possible relevance to depression in a more gene-specific manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is among the most compelling depression-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface between peripheral innate immune activation and central inflammatory signaling. A substantial body of depression research supports the concept that chronic low-grade inflammation, increased cytokine production, and altered gut-microbe or endotoxin-related immune activation contribute to depressive symptomatology in at least a subset of patients. By acting as a key lipopolysaccharide coreceptor and promoting nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells-dependent cytokine production, CD14 provides a mechanistic link between microbial products, systemic inflammation, and downstream neuroimmune effects that can alter monoamine metabolism, glutamatergic signaling, neuroplasticity, and sickness-behavior phenotypes that overlap strongly with depression. Its additional role in responses to modified lipoproteins is also notable, as immunometabolic dysregulation is increasingly recognized in depression. Thus, CD14 stands out as a biologically plausible mediator of inflammation-associated depression and stress-related immune sensitization.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

Extending this inflammatory theme, the next protein appears especially relevant because it may reflect endogenous buffering of cytokine-driven immune activation. IL18BP is highly relevant to depression because it is a natural brake on interleukin 18 signaling, a pathway strongly connected to inflammatory activation, stress biology, and neuroimmune dysfunction. Interleukin 18 is a potent pro-inflammatory cytokine that can amplify T helper type 1 immune responses and potentially influence microglial activation, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity, and neuroplasticity-related pathways implicated in major depressive disorder. In this context, IL18BP may reflect an endogenous compensatory mechanism that buffers excessive inflammatory tone. Proteins that regulate cytokine bioavailability are often particularly informative in depression because they can shape whether inflammatory signals remain adaptive or become chronic and pathological. Therefore, IL18BP stands out as a plausible modulator of inflammation-linked depressive phenotypes, especially in individuals with elevated immune activation.

A related but somewhat broader immunoregulatory profile is seen with LGALS1, which may connect adaptive immune balance to neural plasticity-related processes. LGALS1 (galectin-1) is notable because it integrates immune regulation, cell survival, and inflammatory T-cell polarization, all of which are increasingly implicated in depression pathophysiology. Depression has been associated not only with elevated innate inflammatory markers but also with altered adaptive immune balance, including skewing of T-cell subsets and sustained inflammatory signaling. By promoting T-cell apoptosis and suppressing T helper type 17 differentiation, LGALS1 may influence the chronicity and quality of immune activation. In addition, galectins can modulate cell-cell communication, extracellular matrix interactions, and neuroinflammatory processes that affect synaptic remodeling and stress adaptation. This makes LGALS1 especially interesting as a candidate mediator of the interface between peripheral immune dysregulation and central nervous system plasticity changes observed in depressive disorders.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

Continuing from immune regulation to inflammatory tissue remodeling, CHI3L1 may be relevant where chronic immune activation and altered repair programs are prominent. CHI3L1 is relevant to depression because it is a multifunctional inflammatory and tissue-remodeling factor that may reflect chronic immune activation and altered macrophage polarization. Depression is increasingly conceptualized as involving not only cytokine elevation but also broader dysregulation of immune-cell states, barrier function, and repair programs. CHI3L1 influences dendritic cells, macrophage differentiation, epithelial inflammatory signaling, and stress responses to tissue injury, suggesting a role in systemic inflammatory set points that could secondarily affect the brain. Its involvement in protein kinase B signaling is also noteworthy because phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B-related pathways are linked to neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and antidepressant responses. Accordingly, CHI3L1 may be mechanistically relevant in depression subtypes characterized by inflammation, somatic symptoms, or comorbid metabolic and mucosal dysfunction.

Shifting from cytokine and remodeling pathways to nucleic acid sensing, RNASET2 suggests a possible link between innate immune surveillance and mitochondrial stress biology. RNASET2 stands out because it links innate immune sensing of ribonucleic acid species with endolysosomal toll-like receptor 7 and toll-like receptor 8 activation, pathways that are increasingly discussed in neuroinflammation and stress-related psychiatric disease. Excessive or dysregulated nucleic acid sensing can promote cytokine production and sustained inflammatory states, both of which are associated with depression. Its role in mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover is particularly interesting, since mitochondrial dysfunction and release of mitochondrial danger-associated molecular patterns have been implicated in depressive illness, fatigue syndromes, and stress vulnerability. RNASET2 therefore represents a convergence point between antimicrobial immunity, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammatory signaling, making it biologically plausible in depression mechanisms driven by sterile inflammation or altered immunometabolic regulation.[PubMed:31778653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [PubMed:38697119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [PubMed:28730546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [PubMed:30184494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [PubMed:30385512](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512) 

From innate sensing, the discussion naturally moves to intracellular stress handling and degradative pathways, which are also often implicated in mood disorders. LAMP3 is particularly interesting in depression because disturbed proteostasis, endoplasmic reticulum stress, autophagy, and immunometabolic dysfunction have all been implicated in mood disorders. Chronic stress can impair autophagic flux and increase endoplasmic reticulum stress, which in turn affects neuronal survival, synaptic maintenance, and inflammatory signaling. LAMP3 participates directly in lysosome-autophagosome fusion and the unfolded protein response, positioning it within a cellular stress-response network highly relevant to depression biology. Its possible role in dendritic cell function further broadens its relevance to neuroimmune crosstalk. Thus, LAMP3 may contribute to depression through combined effects on cellular stress adaptation, autophagy-dependent neuronal homeostasis, and immune activation.

A partially overlapping but more vascularly oriented stress pathway is represented by DDAH1, which may connect inflammatory and endothelial mechanisms to depressive symptoms. DDAH1 is relevant to depression because nitric oxide signaling has long been implicated in stress responses, neurovascular regulation, neurotransmission, and inflammatory physiology. By degrading endogenous nitric oxide synthase inhibitors, DDAH1 controls nitric oxide bioavailability, which can influence cerebral blood flow, synaptic signaling, oxidative stress, and endothelial function. These processes are important in depression, especially in vascular depression, late-life depression, and depression associated with cardiometabolic disease. Because asymmetric dimethylarginine accumulation is linked to endothelial dysfunction and inflammation, DDAH1 may also connect depressive symptoms with systemic vascular pathology and altered neurovascular coupling. This makes it a plausible node at the intersection of inflammation, vascular health, and brain function.

Building on this intersection of neural and vascular biology, MDK appears notable because it may integrate neurodevelopmental, inflammatory, and survival-related signaling. MDK is one of the most mechanistically rich proteins in the list with potential relevance to depression because it connects neurodevelopment, neurorepair, inflammation, angiogenesis, and survival signaling. Its actions on neuronal survival, migration, and neurite-related processes suggest possible influence on neural circuit maintenance and plasticity, which are central to depression pathogenesis. Simultaneously, MDK regulates immune-cell recruitment, dendritic-cell programming, and T-cell differentiation, making it a strong candidate mediator of neuroimmune interactions. Its activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B pathways is especially notable, as these pathways are involved in stress adaptation, synaptic plasticity, and antidepressant mechanisms. Furthermore, its role in nitric oxide signaling and vascular responses raises the possibility that MDK contributes to cerebrovascular and inflammatory dimensions of depression.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:1768439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) 

In a similar vein, but with greater emphasis on transcriptional coactivation and growth-related signaling, YAP1 may point toward structural plasticity mechanisms. YAP1 is noteworthy despite the brief annotation because erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 signaling has strong neuropsychiatric relevance, particularly in synaptic development, interneuron function, and cortical circuit regulation. YAP1 is a key transcriptional coactivator in the Hippo pathway, and more broadly it is associated with mechanotransduction, cell survival, and regenerative responses. Through activation of erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 signaling fragments, YAP1 may influence neuronal signaling programs that affect synaptic plasticity and stress responsiveness. Given the established importance of neuroplasticity deficits in depression, proteins capable of modulating growth-factor-related transcriptional responses deserve attention. YAP1 may therefore represent a candidate link between structural plasticity, cellular stress adaptation, and mood-related circuit dysfunction.

The discussion then moves more directly into trophic support for reward-related circuitry, where GFRA1 may be particularly pertinent. GFRA1 is highly relevant to depression because it directly supports dopaminergic neuron survival and differentiation. Dopamine-system dysfunction is strongly implicated in anhedonia, motivational deficits, psychomotor slowing, and reward-processing abnormalities in depression. As a coreceptor for glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, GFRA1 participates in trophic signaling that maintains dopaminergic integrity, suggesting a plausible role in resilience against stress-induced reward-circuit dysfunction. Neurotrophic hypotheses of depression have traditionally emphasized brain-derived neurotrophic factor, but glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor-family pathways are also increasingly recognized as important modulators of mesolimbic and nigrostriatal systems. Accordingly, GFRA1 stands out as a protein with potential relevance to depressive phenotypes involving impaired motivation and reduced reward sensitivity.

A broader tissue and vascular adaptation perspective is introduced by CCN3, which may be relevant where hypoxia-related and angiogenic responses are altered. CCN3 is potentially relevant to depression because it combines roles in angiogenesis, hypoxia signaling, and developmental differentiation. Altered neurovascular function and impaired angiogenic or hypoxia-adaptive responses have been proposed in some forms of depression, particularly where inflammation, metabolic disease, or cerebrovascular burden are present. The ability of CCN3 to modulate hypoxia inducible factor 1 subunit alpha function is especially interesting, as hypoxia-response pathways influence cellular metabolism, stress adaptation, and neuroplasticity. In addition, CCN3 affects proliferation and apoptosis programs, suggesting broader effects on tissue remodeling and possibly neural niche regulation. Its anti-angiogenic activity may be relevant where reduced vascular support contributes to impaired brain plasticity or stress resilience.

This vascular and trophic theme is further reinforced by COL18A1, which may influence angiogenic signaling relevant to both brain perfusion and plasticity. COL18A1 is of interest in depression because vascular and neurovascular abnormalities are increasingly recognized in affective disorders, particularly in late-life depression and treatment-resistant cases with metabolic or inflammatory comorbidity. By antagonizing vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling, COL18A1 may influence angiogenesis, endothelial health, and tissue perfusion. Vascular endothelial growth factor-related pathways are also implicated in adult neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and antidepressant response. Therefore, proteins that suppress vascular endothelial growth factor-mediated signaling may be relevant to depressive states characterized by impaired plasticity or reduced vascular support. Although indirect, the connection is biologically meaningful because depression is not solely a neurotransmitter disorder but also involves trophic and vascular components.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

At the level of cellular stress protection, HSPB6 may offer another perspective on how systemic and neural resilience mechanisms intersect in depression. HSPB6 is relevant to depression because it links cellular stress protection, vascular regulation, and tyrosine 3-monooxygenase and tryptophan 5-monooxygenase activation protein zeta-associated signaling. Molecular chaperones are important in maintaining proteostasis under chronic stress, a condition strongly associated with depression. Its ability to stabilize tyrosine 3-monooxygenase and tryptophan 5-monooxygenase activation protein zeta is notable because 14-3-3 proteins participate in neuronal signaling, synaptic plasticity, and stress-response pathways. In addition, the vascular and cardioprotective functions of HSPB6 may be relevant to the bidirectional relationship between depression and cardiovascular disease. This makes HSPB6 particularly interesting in the context of somatic burden, stress resilience, and systemic physiological dysregulation accompanying depressive illness.

From stress protection, the report then shifts to endocrine signals that can directly shape aversive motivational states and appetite-related behavior. GDF15 is especially relevant to depression because it is a stress-induced endocrine signal that drives aversive motivational states and appetite suppression through defined brainstem circuits. Although it is more directly associated with sickness behavior and anorexia than with depression per se, these phenotypes overlap substantially with core depressive symptoms such as reduced appetite, malaise, fatigue, and behavioral withdrawal. The growth differentiation factor 15-glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor family receptor alpha-like pathway therefore provides a mechanistic framework for how peripheral stressors, inflammation, malignancy, or metabolic drugs can induce central aversive states that resemble aspects of depression. Its activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B pathways in specialized neurons also underscores a structured neurobiological route through which systemic disease may shape mood-related behavior.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

Closely related symptom dimensions are also suggested by NUCB2, particularly with respect to appetite, energy balance, and neuroendocrine regulation. NUCB2 is highly pertinent to depression because appetite and energy-balance disturbances are cardinal symptoms of the disorder. As an anorexigenic factor acting in hypothalamic circuits, NUCB2 may influence motivational and homeostatic systems that are frequently disrupted in depression, including reduced appetite, altered body weight, fatigue, and stress-related autonomic dysregulation. Its potential vascular actions further connect it to the somatic component of mood disorders. Given the growing emphasis on hypothalamic dysfunction and neuroendocrine alterations in depression, NUCB2 stands out as a plausible contributor to symptom dimensions involving appetite suppression and altered energy homeostasis.

Moving from hypothalamic homeostasis to synaptic signaling, NCS1 may be relevant because it directly affects calcium-dependent neuronal plasticity. NCS1 is strongly relevant to depression because it is directly involved in neuronal calcium signaling, G protein-coupled receptor regulation, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal differentiation. Depression is increasingly understood as a disorder of maladaptive plasticity, and proteins that influence calcium-dependent signaling and long-term synaptic change are therefore of high interest. Through its effects on receptor regulation and plasticity-related pathways, NCS1 could modulate neurotransmitter responsiveness and circuit adaptation to stress. Such mechanisms are central to contemporary models of depression and antidepressant action, particularly in relation to synaptic remodeling and altered excitability in limbic networks.

At the level of gene regulation within neurons, RBFOX3 may extend this plasticity-related framework into transcript processing and isoform control. RBFOX3 is relevant because post-transcriptional regulation and alternative splicing are increasingly recognized as important contributors to neuronal identity, synaptic composition, and psychiatric disease risk. Depression has been associated with broad transcriptomic remodeling in cortical and limbic regions, and splicing regulators can exert disproportionate effects by coordinating multiple neuronal gene networks. Although the annotation here is concise, RBFOX-family proteins are central neuronal ribonucleic acid-binding factors, making RBFOX3 a plausible contributor to altered neuronal function, circuit stability, and stress susceptibility in depression. Its importance lies less in a single pathway than in its potential to reprogram neuronal transcript isoforms at scale.

Reintroducing the neuroimmune dimension, TAFA5 may represent a point of convergence between chemokine-like signaling and plasticity-associated kinase pathways. TAFA5 is of interest for depression because it combines chemokine-like signaling with macrophage regulation and protein kinase B and extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway activation. Neuroimmune communication is a major theme in depression biology, and proteins that influence macrophage migration or inflammatory cell behavior may shape systemic and central inflammatory tone. In addition, TAFA family members are often enriched in neural contexts and may participate in neuron-immune crosstalk. Its signaling through G protein-coupled receptors and canonical plasticity-related pathways such as extracellular signal-regulated kinase and protein kinase B further supports its relevance to stress adaptation and mood regulation. TAFA5 may therefore be particularly pertinent to depression subtypes with inflammatory or vascular components.

A more canonical immunoregulatory and remodeling pathway is represented by TGFBR2, which may link cytokine balance to structural adaptation. TGFBR2 is highly relevant to depression because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a major regulator of immunosuppression, tissue remodeling, extracellular matrix biology, and cellular stress responses. Depression has been linked to altered cytokine networks that include not only pro-inflammatory mediators but also dysregulated counter-regulatory pathways. Through canonical and non-canonical signaling, TGFBR2 can influence immune tolerance, glial function, extracellular matrix composition, and structural plasticity, all of which may affect brain resilience to chronic stress. This receptor therefore represents a plausible mechanistic bridge between inflammation, maladaptive remodeling, and impaired recovery processes in depression.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) 

Within the adaptive immune compartment, TNFRSF9 may further indicate how immune-cell energetic state and survival could intersect with depressive pathophysiology. TNFRSF9 is relevant to depression because it reflects adaptive immune activation and mitochondrial regulation in T cells, both of which have become important themes in immunopsychiatry. Depression has been associated with altered T-cell phenotypes, immune exhaustion in some contexts, and broad mitochondrial dysfunction. A receptor that strengthens T-cell survival and mitochondrial activity may therefore influence the quality of peripheral immune responses that feed back onto the brain through cytokines and metabolic mediators. While the connection is indirect, TNFRSF9 stands out as a marker of immune-cell energetic state and immune competence, which may be altered in inflammatory depression.

Finally, ACVRL1 returns the discussion to endothelial and transforming growth factor beta-family signaling, providing a fitting conclusion to the broader neurovascular and immunoregulatory themes in this protein set. ACVRL1 is potentially relevant to depression because it intersects angiogenesis and transforming growth factor beta-family signaling, two systems increasingly implicated in neurovascular health and stress adaptation. Endothelial dysfunction and impaired vascular remodeling may contribute to depressive symptoms, especially in aging, vascular comorbidity, and inflammatory states. Through SMAD family member 1-dependent signaling in endothelial cells, ACVRL1 may influence cerebrovascular integrity and trophic support. Its relation to transforming growth factor beta signaling further strengthens its relevance, as this cytokine family modulates inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and neural repair. Thus, ACVRL1 may contribute to depression through neurovascular and immunoregulatory mechanisms rather than classical neurotransmitter pathways.
